Business.title: ‘It’s not helping’: calls for guardrails and regulations as AI use rises at US retailers
Business.text:
As millions of Americans begin holiday shopping this Black Friday, consumers and workers alike are already seeing how artificial intelligence is reshaping the retail landscape.

Anna, a cashier in a southern Oregon Walmart and leader with United for Respect, who requested to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, criticized the implementation of AI at Walmart and its effects on workers.

According to Anna, AI is used for human resources tasks such as scheduling, assigning attendance disciplinary points, and through a safety alert system that she says is often inaccurate and often pulls her away from customer service interactions.

“During the course of a day on a given shift, I will get at least 10 or 15 safety alerts on my phone. I can’t move on through the app until the safety alert’s clear.” she said. “It’s very annoying when you get them. I need to go over here to help this young lady who’s crying her eyeballs out because she needs a pregnancy test, and I can’t get in to get her pregnancy test because I have to clear a stupid alert.”

She explained she has to take a photo and upload it after completing a safety alert, noting alerts can often mistake a shadow, a sticker, or something else as an actionable item, or will be flagged to an associate when it is a maintenance issue.

“If there is something that I clearly see that is on the floor, I’m going to pick it up. I’m not that ignorant to not to pick it up, but I don’t need an AI telling me to do it,” she added. “It’s not helping. This thing is supposed to be working with us and to help us and things like that. I don’t see how this is, because it’s not.”

In September 2026, several hundred Walmart workers had signed on to an open letter calling for the company to put workers first as it rolls out the use of AI in stores.

Walmart investors overwhelmingly voted down a proposal for a report on how the Walmart workplace is being affected by AI and automation in June 2026. A Walmart spokesperson cited an internal June 2026 survey where 84% of Walmart workers claimed they were confident using digital tools.

“Walmart’s approach to AI is, and always has been, people-led and tech-powered,” a Walmart spokesperson said in an email. “We use AI to serve our customers and members and better support associates – not to replace their judgment, experience, or expertise. Like any technology, these tools evolve over time, and feedback from the associates who use them helps us continually improve the experience and build practical tools that are useful on the floor.”

The use and implementation of AI in the retail industry is expected to continue to grow, according to industry leaders.

According to a survey of 56 AI leaders at US-based retailers published in December 2025 by the National Retail Federation, most retailers have or are implementing AI in a variety of uses, with plans to increase investments and implementation over the next few years.

About 75% of retailers surveyed reported implementing AI tools for coding and app development, 73% for office productivity tools, 66% for cybersecurity and fraud development, 59% reported preparing or implementing AI for supply chain and warehouse operations, and 45% reported doing so for marketing and advertising.

As AI use is becoming more commonplace, labor leaders and advocates have called for guardrails and regulations to protect workers and consumers, and protections in collective bargaining agreements to ensure workers have a say in AI use and implementation in their workplaces.

“Without proper guardrails, AI systems have supercharged surveillance for both consumers and for the workers who make it possible for consumers to buy what they need or what they want for their loved ones for the holiday season,” said Crystal Weise, policy & programs director at the AFL-CIO Tech Institute, a non-profit labor hub started by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of unions in the US.

Weise noted surveillance of workers starts at the factories and warehouses where consumer goods are manufactured and distributed, to surveillance of consumers online and in stores, who have their shopping habits tracked and influenced by algorithms, and of workers, with these surveillance systems fueled by AI.

“We know that these surveillance technologies make jobs worse, and we know that it makes products and services more expensive. We need policies and collective bargaining agreements that stop exploitative surveillance,” she added. “We want to see humans in control of how shoppers and consumers are accessing the goods and services that they need.”

Weise said AI-fueled surveillance systems such as surveillance pricing, productivity quotas on workers, and monitoring dissent and workplace organizing efforts are already collecting reams of valuable data on workers and consumers, which is used to cut costs and drive up profit margins.

Shoppers may be subjected to AI before they even walk into a brick-and-mortar store, with several major retailers such as Macy’s, Target, Home Depot and Costco using automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and other retailers using AI tools to scale back Black Friday discounts and bolster their profit margins.

“We use this technology for limited, authorized purposes. Data is collected through ALPRs to prevent theft and fraud, help ensure security, and maintain the safety of individuals and our properties,” states Macy’s disclaimer notice on the use of the technology at some stores.

For workers, they may be subjected to AI from the beginning of applying for a job, such as at Amazon-owned Whole Foods, which uses an AI recruiting agent named Sage – the only way to apply for a job at the company, according to Whole Foods’ website on job applications.

Once in stores, customers and workers can be subjected to AI facial recognition technology, with major retailers such as Wegmans, Macy’s and Home Depot citing use of the technology, and customers are having their data collected by major retailers, such as Kroger, which archives data it collects on customers and sells it, according to a 2025 Consumer Reports investigation.

“We’re not anti-technology, but we are anti-dehumanization of the workplace,” said Stuart Appelbaum, president of the Retail, Wholesale, and Department Store Union and executive vice-president of the United Food and Commercial Workers.

Appelbaum argued AI can’t measure or be aware of life situations that should be accounted for in decisions related to discipline or job termination, and cited negative effects of algorithmic surveillance on workers.

“We’ve seen a rise in algorithmic surveillance, and it creates a pressure cooker environment. People are afraid to pause for a breath, or even to go to the bathroom, and for us, that’s really workplace harassment by algorithm,” he said. “Every worker deserves to have a human involved before any discipline takes place.”

He cited contracts the union has won at employers that include protections on how AI is used and implemented in workplaces, and emphasized the importance of being able to bargain over new technologies as employers are frequently using AI to try to lower labor costs and increase profit margins.

“A lot of retailers are using AI as an excuse to have fewer people on the shop floor,” Appelbaum added. “What you end up doing is diminishing the in-store experience, and I think that’s a huge mistake. Not only does it put pressure on the people who remain working, but it also, I think, isn’t good for the future of the store. Basically, we think the technology should be used to empower and strengthen retail workers, and I think that’s part and parcel of everything we negotiate.”

Fears of large-scale layoffs in the retail industry thanks to AI have yet to materialize. According to a July 2026 policy brief published by Stanford University researchers, AI’s impact on overall employment is “likely small” at the moment. But several firms have announced planned job cuts over the next few years, citing AI or AI investments as a leading factor, and new technologies, such as electronic shelf labels, are projected to result in job losses and increase prices for consumers.

In October 2026, Kroger announced plans to cut 3,000 corporate jobs over the next three years, citing the use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.

“These notifications are part of the corporate headcount reduction the company announced in early October to lower prices and improve the shopping experience by simplifying operations and better use of technology,” said a Kroger spokesperson on the cuts.

The announcement came after the company was hit with a charge of $2.6bn in 2025 following its decision to shut down three automated robotic delivery centers, which Kroger did not comment on.

“As retailers feel the pressure from Wall Street to cut costs and pump up share prices, they’re turning to AI to do the dirty work,” said Milton Jones, international president of the United Food and Commercial Workers, which represents workers at around two-thirds of Kroger stores in the US. “Whether it’s AI-powered scheduling that slashes retail workers’ hours or surveillance pricing that raises costs for consumers, people are getting squeezed on both sides of the cash register.”

Bryan Wynn, national bargaining director for the United Food and Commercial Workers, said that investors are pushing for artificial intelligence investments at firms to cut labor costs, increase efficiencies, boost profits, largely without concerns for how these technologies affected workers and consumers.

He explained planning for these technologies has exceedingly become a concern in bargaining contract renewals and future union contracts, as retail employers are using AI for data collection and surveillance to influence and monitor the behaviors of workers and consumers, and to use that data to further increase profits.

“People should have a say in how AI and their data are used to change how they work and shop,” added Jones. “We need technology that works for our members, and all working people, not automation that steals their livelihoods.”

Business.title: Amazon’s sale deals deceive customers, thinktank alleges
Business.text:
An Apple Watch on sale for $680. A pair of women’s Hunter yellow rainboots discounted for $127, and a pair of men’s UGG boots, $180. A Carhartt beanie just shy of $20.

These discounts – all reportedly featured last year on Amazon’s own curation of its best Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals – sound like good deals for the holiday gift season. But a recent analysis from progressive thinktank Groundwork Collaborative found these products and others had been listed at the same price or even less just days before Amazon started advertising them as discounted.

Overall, researchers found that about 30% of the products Amazon highlighted for its Black Friday and Cyber Monday campaigns were priced the same or even lower in the month before the sale. That share increased to 60% when extending the timeline to 60 days prior to the sale events. Across the board, median sale prices were actually nearly 20% higher than their pre-Black Friday offering.

Those Hunter rainboots, for example, were listed for nearly $50 less – about $80 – just nine days before going on its advertised “sale” Groundwork said. The Apple Watch and men’s UGG boots were both listed for roughly $80 less within a month of the Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales of last year.

It was the “most rigorous, intensive project” that the thinktank had taken on in its history, Lindsay Owens, the president and chief executive of Groundwork, said after the report’s release.

“Americans are really squeezed right now. Back-to-school shopping was expensive. Buying a Thanksgiving meal for your family is going to be expensive. Holiday gift shopping is going to be really expensive,” Owens said in an interview with the Guardian. “Sale events are a really important way that families stretch their dollars, and Americans trust that these Amazon sales events and other sales events around Black Friday and Cyber Monday are worth waiting for, and offer them genuine savings.

“Our report suggests otherwise,” she continued, “that the sale events aren’t always what they’re cracked up to be.”

Amazon said in a statement on its website that the Groundwork Collaborative published “deeply flawed and false claims” and that it “cherrypicked” findings.

“This is the second attempt that Groundwork has made in the past week to assert false claims about our deal events based on flawed methodology and inaccurate data, and it’s clear they have no interest in the facts and are focused on pursuing a pre-determined narrative,” said in the statement.

In further statements to the Guardian, Amazon said that it analyzed deals from the report’s claims and found that 98% of the products in 2024 and 99% of products in 2024 were at the same price or lower over the past 30 days from the sale events.

“When we looked at the research’s actual deals for 2025, we found that 89% of the products had lower prices and 10% were the same, compared with the prior 30-day low prices,” the company said. “Groundwork’s research appears to focus on two low-trafficked corporate blog pages that inadvertently listed some products as deals and was clearly marked as subject to change. Groundwork is basing this misleading claim on a handful of these products that were mistakenly included on those pages but were not badged as deals in our store.”

For products that were accurately labeled as deals, consumers saved an average of more than 35% off list price, the company said.

The report comes as Americans say they are facing higher prices across the board, especially for gas and groceries. Companies have also come under increased scrutiny over unfair pricing practices, including dynamic and surveillance pricing, which Owen has further scrutinized in her recent book, Gouged.

Other governments have made efforts to crack down on unfair pricing practices, especially during Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals. Earlier this month, the European Commission proposed a new ban to regulate certain practices such as on “dark pattern” marketing tactics that falsely claim a product is almost sold out to pressure consumers into purchasing the item. The proposal, which is now under review by the European parliament and council, also threatens companies with fines if they push consumers to buy more or target minors with personalized advertising.

“It’s time for Congress to put Amazon executives in the hot seat and make them come clean about their pricing games,” Elizabeth Pancotti, the Groundwork Collaborative’s vice-president of policy, advocacy and research, said in a news conference after the report was released last week. “And the [Federal Trade Commission] should not wait to resume enforcement of its deceptive pricing guide, which has laid dormant for 50 years, and issue formal rule-making with real teeth.”

Business.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
Business.text:
Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency.

The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December.

“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.

“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun.

Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties”.

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also earmarked for new tariffs but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products that account for ​more than 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the EU, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will probably support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However, the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos”.

He added: “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

With Associated Press and Reuters

Business.title: Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses
Business.text:
The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network sued the agency in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.

The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.

At a hearing early last month, AliKhan seemed skeptical of the FCC’s reasoning for the early renewal order.

In her ruling, the judge said that ABC is “likely to succeed on their first amendment claim” of retaliation.

In addition to granting ABC’s request for a preliminary injunction, the judge denied the FCC’s request to dismiss the case. But she also denied ABC’s request to prevent the FCC from taking “any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten plaintiffs with sanctions in an effort to alter their exercise of editorial discretion”.

In her ruling, the judge acknowledged the seriousness of the possible penalties facing ABC – and the chilling effect produced by an early license renewal order on a news organization’s first amendment rights. “Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face – loss of their broadcast licenses – the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness,” she wrote. “Any broadcaster of ordinary firmness – wealthy or not – would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business.”

The judge highlighted Trump’s long-standing animus against ABC as a clear factor in the FCC’s actions. “Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now,” she wrote, adding that the chairperson, Brendan Carr, “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders”.

As for the timing of the early renewal order request, coming soon after Trump’s criticism of Kimmel, the judge wrote: “Against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”

The judge also noted the odd timing of the early renewal order, coming more than a year after the FCC began investigating ABC. And she acknowledged as credible the network’s concern that the agency’s license review process could run indefinitely.

“The existence of other mechanisms to solicit public input, coupled with the untenable timeline, casts serious doubt on the argument that Defendants are using the early license renewal proceedings to enhance public participation,” she wrote. “All told, the ‘significant mismatch’ between Defendants’ decision to order the proceedings when they did and their stated rationale for doing so presents an air of pretext the court will not ignore.”

In a statement, an ABC News spokesperson said: “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration.”

Anna M Gomez, the lone FCC commissioner appointed by a Democratic president, also celebrated the judge’s ruling. “This decision shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights,” she said in a statement. “For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct. That brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control. Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I’ve said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side.”

“While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law – as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear,” a FCC spokesperson said in a statement. “The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”

Sports.title: Wesley Fofana: Chelsea defender booed by own fans in defeat by Nottingham Forest
Sports.text:
Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana was subjected to repeated boos and told "you're not welcome here" by his own fans during Friday's Premier League defeat by Nottingham Forest.

The jeers aimed at the 25-year-old were heard every time he touched the ball and came after an unauthorised interview with French YouTuber Zach Nani was released.

In that controversial two-hour conversation, Fofana also appeared to joke about missing his penalty during last month's Carabao Cup shootout defeat by Liverpool.

Manager Xabi Alonso said the French centre-back had apologised and "it won't be repeated".

But Fofana endured a difficult time in his side's trip to Forest as supporters made their feelings known.

After Chelsea went behind to a brilliant volley from Igor Jesus in the fifth minute, Fofana also conceded a penalty for the home side's second goal from Morgan Gibbs-White in the 51st minute.

He was booked for the foul on Liam Delap in the box, and then replaced by Levi Colwill in the 56th minute - just after Emmanuel Emegha had pulled a goal back for the visitors - before Gibbs-White made it 3-1 in the 72nd minute.

Emegha scored again in the 89th minute to make it 3-2, but Forest held on to secure their first win over Chelsea at the City Ground since 1997.

Alonso defended Fofana after the game and said in his post-match news conference: "We have to stick together, and everyone that is in the changing room, everyone in the team is needed.

"We need to help, and we need to go through these tough moments all together, and we don't leave anyone apart.

"We need to support everyone. That is because we need everyone, and we need the fans.

"We need all the players. We need to stick together because if not, things will get more complicated, and that's what we want to do."

Sports.title: Chapecoense: 10 years on - how team rebuilt after 2016 plane crash
Sports.text:
It was 2am when Ivan Tozzo picked up his mobile phone and heard his football club's secretary screaming his name.

A plane carrying the Chapecoense team had crashed into a mountain.

Seventy-one people were dead, including 19 of 22 players from the Brazilian club who were on their way to the biggest game in their history.

It would later emerge the plane had run out of fuel and investigators would find the airline and pilot were to blame as the fuel load was insufficient for the flight on 28 November 2016.

But in the early hours, as Tozzo watched the TV news in the changing room at the club's stadium, his only thought was for the players who would not be coming back to this room.

When he sat alone in the club's boardroom after the funerals as the only director still alive, he cried.

That was the moment when Tozzo – who had changed his mind about travelling with the team because he had a sense of unease about the trip - decided he would lead Chapecoense to rise again.

Chapecoense had been travelling to Colombia to play Atletico Nacional of Medellin in the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana final, South America's second most prestigious club tournament.

It was a first continental final for the Brazilian team.

"The team was very motivated, knowing that we were engraving our names inside the history of the club," goalkeeper Jakson Follmann, one of the three surviving players, tells BBC Sport.

Aged 24 at the time, Follmann had also been looking forward to his imminent wedding, little knowing he would be spending two months in hospital instead.

"Everyone was completely proud of everything they were doing, both for the team and for the community of Chapeco and the region," Follmann says.

Commentator Rafael Henzel, who was one of six survivors of the crash but who died in 2019 following a heart attack, described the Copa Sudamericana as the team's "World Cup" and said in 2017 that "if anyone's ever died happy, it was the people on that plane".

The LaMia 2933 flight from Santa Cruz in Bolivia to the Colombian city of Medellin had a journey distance similar to the plane's flying range, but it did not stop to refuel and crashed into a mountain just 18km from its intended destination.

The pilot, Miguel Quiroga, who was also a co-owner of the airline, died in the crash. In a leaked tape, he can be heard warning of a "total electric failure" and "lack of fuel". However, he did not make a formal distress call.

A Bolivian investigation concluded that the pilot and the airline were directly responsible for the crash, while a Colombian investigation said there was no technical failure and blamed the pilot, the airline and Bolivian regulators.

"I don't call it an accident, I say it was a crime that could have been avoided," says Follman, whose right leg had to be partially amputated to save his life.

"It's the crime of not stopping to refuel, the greed to think that he [the pilot] could get there... with the fuel practically finished."

To date, no-one has been found guilty in relation to the crash.

At the time, Bolivia did not have a system for prosecuting companies. Even when such a facility was introduced in 2021, it did not cover negligent homicide or causing an air disaster.

Charges were brought against individuals in LaMia's management - who denied wrongdoing - but in 2020 a trial was delayed by jurisdictional disputes and difficulties involving defendants who were abroad.

Seven thousand kilometres away in the small southern Brazilian city of Chapeco, Tozzo watched the scale of the disaster unfold on TV screens at the stadium in the middle of the night.

"At five o'clock in the morning, the players' wives began to arrive. It was despair. People threw themselves on the ground and cried," says Tozzo, a local entrepreneur who was the club's vice-president at the time and had joined the club in 2009 when they were not even playing in Brazil's national football pyramid.

Two days earlier, Tozzo had suffered misgivings about the trip that were so strong that he had changed his mind about travelling to Medellin.

"It was a thing from God. It was not for me to go. I called [financial director] Decio, who organised all our trips, and I told him that I would not go," he says.

"He went crazy with me. 'Why? You agreed to go, now you do not want to go? You have to go.'

"My sister was next to me, saying, 'You need to go to this match, you worked so hard to get to this moment.' But in my head I said, 'No Ivan, I will not go', and I stayed at home."

After the crash, he had another strong feeling about his path.

"I think I had a mission here on Earth to continue Chapecoense after the accident," Tozzo says. "I was the only one of the directors left alive so I took over as [interim] president."

A sleepless week followed in which Tozzo arranged flights to Colombia for doctors, relatives and pastors to identify and recover the remains and be with the survivors.

A memorial service was organised and, in pouring rain, the coffins were brought into Chape's stadium, Arena Conda.

During the service came the news that Atletico Nacional had asked for the Copa Sudamericana trophy and winners' prize money to be awarded to Chapecoense.

Then came the question of the future.

Tozzo was determined Chapecoense would compete again, but none of the surviving players were in any shape to play and they only had two other squad members – who did not travel to Medellin because of injury – and a handful in the academy.

They called on Rui Costa, who had been sacked by Gremio as football director six months earlier and accepted the same role with Chapecoense, and appointed Vagner Mancini as coach.

In a matter of weeks, 22 new players were signed, most of them on loan.

Tozzo's message rang clear in the ears of the new players.

"Our fans were very sad, Chapecoense was very sad, and playing again with joy was not easy," he says.

"We explained very well the responsibility they would have."

It was time to return to the pitch.

Chapecoense's first match back – eight weeks after the crash – was a friendly against the last team the club had played, Palmeiras.

Before the game at the Arena Conda, Follmann – in a wheelchair – was joined by Neto and the other surviving player, Alan Ruschel, to receive the Copa Sudamericana trophy.

Fireworks lit up the sky.

"It was the first time I had gone back to the arena, the first time I really had contact with people, because I was still hospitalised," says Follmann.

"When I received the trophy, a movie went through my head because our captain Cleber Santana should have been holding it surrounded by all of us, celebrating."

The friendly against Palmeiras was the first of 80 matches that Chapecoense played in 2017, only five of them friendlies.

There was an offer from the Brazilian Football Confederation to give the club immunity from relegation for three seasons, but Tozzo rejected it.

"How can you psych up the players to play their best if they know that their classification is guaranteed?" he asks.

As it turned out, Chapecoense stayed up on their own merits for precisely three seasons.

In 2017, as Sudamericana champions, they once again had to face Atletico Nacional, the reigning Copa Libertadores winners, in the South American Super Cup.

It meant another flight to Medellin just months after the crash. This time Tozzo was on board.

"We went to see the exact location [of the crash]," he says. "I can't believe it was so close [to the airport]."

Chapecoense lost 6-3 on aggregate but later in the year won their state championship and finished as high as eighth in the national league in a demonstration of remarkable resilience.

The following year, in the second wave of new players, defender Bruno Pacheco was signed.

Pacheco, who has made nearly 150 appearances for the club in two spells, says: "Stepping on to the pitch at the arena was an emotional experience.

"I was representing those who are no longer with us, as well as the fans. I'm happy to be part of such an important chapter in the club's history."

After relegation from Serie A in 2019, Chapecoense won the Serie B title to earn promotion back to the top flight.

But that lasted just one season and they spent the next four terms in the second tier. They have spent this year in Serie A but will be relegated again.

After the crash, Neto's only appearance for Chapecoense came as a substitute in a charity friendly in December 2017, when money was raised to support relatives of the victims.

He remained at the club as a player for two more years until being forced to retire by the pain of his crash-related injuries.

He became a Christian evangelist, and he speaks for the relatives of his former team-mates who are still seeking justice as some families pursue compensation and hold out hope for criminal convictions.

Left-back Ruschel, who suffered severe injuries and had spinal surgery, was the only player to continue his professional playing career meaningfully, returning to the game nine months after the crash and staying with Chapecoense until 2021.

He only retired this November, helping his side Juventude win promotion to Serie A in his final game, ironically to swap places with Chapecoense.

Neto presented him with a commemorative plaque at half-time in Chapecoense's game against Palmeiras at the Arena Conda on 24 November when both men held aloft a jersey bearing Follmann's name.

Ruschel referenced the plane crash in a video announcing his retirement, calling it "a day that changed my life forever".

"I lost friends, companions and people with whom I shared dreams and projects," he said.

"And God gave me a second chance. I didn't know if I would be able to play football again, but I believed that if I was here, there was still a purpose for my life.

"And today, I have the privilege of being able to choose the moment to say goodbye."

Follmann's wedding - the one he had been preparing for before the crash - did happen and he became a father.

Despite having an offer to join Brazil's sitting volleyball team at the Paralympics, he turned to careers as a singer, motivational speaker and author, but with a new perspective.

"I observe everything around me. I observe life," he says.

"I have issues with making plans for the future, because life showed me that I only have today to live.

"I don't leave anything for tomorrow. I say everything today. I forgive today, I hug today."

Tozzo, the director who stayed at home, continues to live in Chapeco where he runs various businesses.

"I haven't talked about the accident for a long time," he says. "We keep remembering, and every time we talk, tears fall, but these are things in life that we have to face."

Additional reporting by Julia Dias Carneiro

Sports.title: Are Freddy, Zak and Luca Carrick-Smith British skiing's next family dynasty?
Sports.text:
It is the rarest of sights.

Three Britons on a skiing podium, the union jack emblazoned across their race bibs as they lift their skis in celebration.

And then you learn they all have the same surname.

At a slalom race in New Zealand in September, Luca, Freddy and Zak Carrick-Smith completed a sibling clean sweep of the medals, something no three brothers are believed to have ever done before in the history of FIS alpine skiing.

"It was super special," Freddy tells BBC Sport. "The goal is to do the same thing at a World Cup or the Olympics now."

Their success came at the start of a winter season in which the brothers hope to solidify their burgeoning potential as British alpine skiing's next big things.

And could they follow in the grooves of Olympians Graham and Martin Bell, and Alain and Noel Baxter, to become GB's next family skiing dynasty?

Freddy, 19, is on GB's World Cup squad, while his twin Zak and older brother Luca, 21, are on the second-tier Europa Cup team.

And with their parents as their coaches, it is a full family affair.

The boys' mother Emma Carrick-Anderson was a four-time Winter Olympian for Team GB, while father Phil Smith founded Snoworks ski courses, which operate across Europe.

"They know us best, so they know us much better than just a random coach would," says Zak.

"And then as brothers, me and Freddy have been racing our whole lives together, pushing each other, and then Luca ahead pushing us too. I think that's why we've got so far."

Luca adds: "The best part of it probably, for us, is the competition, and I always want to be the best in everything, especially when we grew up.

"Everything you did, you'd always be pushing harder and harder. We all get along really well, and it's just like being with your best friends all the time.

"It's always been pretty incredible, but it has been difficult at times."

Emma is matter-of-fact about that challenge. Asked what was behind the decision to go it alone as a family, she said: "Basically we didn't have a choice. Ski racing is incredibly expensive.

"When the boys were young, it was all just fun. I don't think we really planned that we were going to take this journey to where we are now, knocking on the World Cup door.

"We would never have been able to afford to put them in an academy. So I think we were lucky, I was an ex-ski racer, Phil was a ski racer, we were also ski coaches, so we could do it ourselves. Not all families are quite as lucky."

Each season, they must source about £320,000. Last season, they feared they would run out of money by mid-January.

While some of their funding comes through GB Snowsport and its Alpine Foundation, the rest must be found through sponsorship deals and crowdfunding campaigns.

When BBC Sport speaks to Emma, she is in Colorado with Freddy, where he will race in the giant slalom World Cup this weekend.

There, a two-and-a-half-hour training session on the slopes costs $1,200 (£914). Fortunately, they are able to split that cost with other teams, but with Luca in Finland and Zak in Austria, Emma and Phil - who quit their jobs a number of years ago - effectively run three different programmes.

Coaches, ski techs, fitness instructors, course-setters, drivers, cooks - they have done plenty of jobs on their sons' journeys up the rankings.

Emma describes them as completely different personalities, and yet "all incredibly determined in their own way". But managing the emotions of her three sons as they learn to navigate the ups and downs of professional sport has been the parents' hardest role.

"They're our kids first, so they're humans first before athletes. And I think that's so important because that will help you ride out the tough times," says Emma.

"I was an athlete myself, and it's very difficult sometimes to separate Emma from the ski racer.

"That is something I know a lot of people struggle with, but it's something that we've been really working on with our guys. You know, if you have a bad result, it doesn't matter. You're not a bad person."

Thankfully, there hasn't been much in the way of bad results for the Carrick-Smiths so far this season - and Freddy in particular has enjoyed a dream start to the winter.

In October, in the first giant slalom World Cup of the season in Solden, Austria, he finished 12th - the best-ever result by a British man in the discipline at that level.

After the first run, he was in 21st place - and so hard were his celebrations at that point that he snapped a pole.

Zak and Luca were watching his second run from the finish area, while Emma was watching from the wings and Phil from the start gate. Freddy recorded the fifth-fastest time of the day to rise nine places in the standings.

"It gives me a lot of confidence," he said. "I think I knew I had it in me, but after last year's performance in the World Cup [when he failed to qualify for the second run], I wasn't so sure.

"But I was feeling good going into the race, and I thought I could get into the top 30 and have a good second run, so I thought it was possible."

The campaign continues Stateside for Freddy this weekend in Copper Mountain. Only securing his place on the startline after his success in Solden, it is an unexpected yet welcome twist early on in the season - at an added cost of £20,000 that had not been budgeted for.

"We just keep going. You keep going, keep being positive," says Emma. "Things like Freddy's results. it just makes you realise how incredibly far we've come."

And yet they hope there is further to go. Asked about their ultimate goal, twin telepathy comes to the fore.

"We want to be the best in the world," Freddy and Zak say in unison.

Sports.title: Nations Championship: Five-try Ireland beat Australia in autumn finale
Sports.text:
Nations Championship

Tries: Henshaw, Timoney, Baloucoune, McNabney 2 Cons: Prendergast 5 Pen: Prendergast

Tries: Williams, Thomas Cons: Gordon 2

Ireland secured a fifth-place finish in the inaugural Nations Championship thanks to a 38-14 victory over Australia in London.

While last week's 20-17 win over South Africa was the undoubted highlight of their campaign, victory on Friday night ensured Ireland won all four games they played in November.

After Italy narrowly beat Fiji in the first game of the day, Ireland started slowly in a sparsely populated Allianz Stadium with the Wallabies taking a deserved lead through Jeremy Williams' try.

Andy Farrell's side took control of the contest through 24 unanswered points either side of half-time with Robbie Henshaw, Nick Timoney and Robert Baloucoune crossing for scores, while Sam Prendergast converted all three and added a penalty.

Kalani Thomas briefly stalled Ireland's momentum, but replacement back row James McNabney marked his second cap with a pair of tries in the final seven minutes to give the number two side in the world a comfortable, if not always convincing, victory.

After what was their final Test match of 2026, Ireland finish the year with a record of 10 wins and two losses from 12 internationals.

After making only two forced changes from the side who beat the Springboks six days ago - the banned Dan Sheehan and ill Mack Hansen the ones to miss out - head coach Farrell had called on his squad to back up their performance against the reigning world champions.

The early stages, however, had none of the tempo or accuracy from last week in the Aviva Stadium. Sloppy knock-ons, coupled with a pair of scrum penalties, saw Ireland struggle to gain a foothold in the contest.

For all Australia's territory and possession, the Wallabies took until the 23rd minute to press home their advantage on the scoreboard.

Previously undone by a couple of kicking errors, Les Kiss' side looked most dangerous when keeping the ball tight and it was lock Williams who burrowed over for the game's opening score.

Australia's deserved lead, however, lasted just three minutes. A midfield penalty allowed Prendergast to kick for the corner and give Ireland their first visit to the opposition 22.

After a sharp attack down the short side was thwarted before the line, Ireland came back inside and Stuart McCloskey spun out of a tackle well to put his centre partner Henshaw over for the try.

Three minutes before the break, again aided by an Australia penalty, Ireland doubled their lead.

Tadhg Beirne did well to gather a line-out with one hand and, with Ireland's centres joining the maul, number eight Timoney broke off the base for the simple score.

Prendergast converted both scores and added a penalty with the last kick of the half to put Ireland in a commanding 10-point lead at the break despite their shaky start.

Sports.title: England v New Zealand: Nations Championship game chance for All Blacks to arrest decline
Sports.text:
For decades, the All Blacks have defied gravity.

Despite a population, player pool and bank balance smaller than most of their rivals, New Zealand's rugby team have become sporting shorthand for success.

Deservedly so. No other team comes close to them.

England beat the All Blacks this year and last. They play them again on Saturday aiming for a hat-trick.

But, England would need that winning streak to continue until around 2050 just to level up a lop-sided historical head-to-head.

New Zealand have won 36 times to England's 10 in their 121-year rivalry.

For every other nation in Test rugby, the story is the same. New Zealand have the superior record against them all.

A section on the All Blacks' website, titled Rivalries,, external opens by listing South Africa's 40% winning record in their meetings. And the numbers only drop from there.

But New Zealand's grip on the global game appears looser now than ever.

If they lose to England on Saturday, it may not much sway the historical balance between the two teams.

But it would be a sixth defeat in a calendar year, a total matched only once before in the All Blacks past, back in 1949 when a split squad played two Test series in Australia and apartheid South Africa at the same time.

This current crop of All Blacks are suffering not just by comparison to the previous generation, but when set against every other modern predecessor.

One reason may be a source of strength turning against them.

The All Blacks' culture of promoting within and establishing coaching dynasties was seen as key when they were winning.

A thread ran through the Graham Henry, Steve Hansen and Ian Foster succession in the 2010s glory days. The latter two served under their predecessor and the first two earned their Test stripes with Wales, before taking the top job.

All were schooled as coaches in New Zealand and steeped in the country's rugby traditions.

The in-house production line of leaders ensured continuity and protected a team ethos that has been admired and written about everywhere.

But, in a modern world in which opposition tactics are quickly picked apart and best practice spreads fast, has adherence to tradition held back the team?

New Zealand's rivals have all hired coaching talent from outside.

Rassie Erasmus, South African to the core, may front the Springbok coaching operation, but behind him Irishmen Jerry Flannery and Felix Jones and Tony Brown, a former All Black himself, bring specialist knowledge to different areas.

France, famously patriotic in their hiring, benefited from Englishman Shaun Edwards and South African Vlok Cilliers' work behind the scenes in recent years.

England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales all have or have had head coaches from other countries.

Dave Rennie, who has coached Australia, Glasgow Warriors and Japanese side Kobe Steelers previously, became the first person of Pasifika heritage to lead the All Blacks when he took on the job in March.

He has brought a Scottish contingent to mix up his backroom, with attack coach Mike Blair the most high-profile.

But his regime is still only eight months old. Other issues predate it.

Most pressing is the balance sheet.

New Zealand Rugby is leaking millions. A failure to balance the books means it has built-in annual losses of about NZ$20m (£8.35m), and is projected to lose NZ$66m (£27.6m) between 2027 and 2031., external

The All Black brand is valuable. It has been licensed to sell watches, healthcare and information technology.

The team are still a powerful global draw.

They are among the keenest Test nations to play matches overseas, where they can fill stadiums bigger than Auckland's 50,000-capacity Eden Park and make more money.

A globe-trotting 2026 itinerary has filled coffers, but emptied players.

Still though costs are rising faster than their income.

In turn, that is compromising the All Blacks' ability to keep their centrally contracted stars at home.

As in England, playing for a domestic team is a requirement to play internationally.

Thirty-five-year-old playmaker Beauden Barrett's proposed move to Bristol Bears and out of eligibility at the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup attracted headlines, but New Zealand are more concerned by other departures.

Back-row star Wallace Sititi, 24, is rumoured to have agreed a move to Stade Francais, while Luke Jacobson, 29, has already announced his own switch to fellow French side Bayonne.

"What bothers us is when All Blacks or highly prospective All Blacks leave in their sort of mid-20s," said New Zealand Rugby chairman and World Cup-winning captain David Kirk this week., external

"When they want to go away for two or three years or something like that in their mid-20s, possibly come back, but possibly not come back. That's a problem for us.

"We're not ever going to win on the money. We just don't have the money to compete with Japan and France, who are the two big payers.

"So we have to compete on the desire to play for the All Blacks and to have a career that's memorable representing New Zealand. And most of the time that's absolutely fine.

"That's why the few people leaving become a bit of a cause célèbre - because not many do."

Richie Mo'unga is one of them.

He was New Zealand's first-choice fly-half at the last World Cup and arguably the best in the position in the world.

He spent three years in Japanese club rugby and international exile afterwards, and has yet to fully find his feet on his return.

New Zealand have the talent to cope. Ruben Love is a coming force at 10. Many of their stars will time stints overseas around World Cups. But it robs them of options and makes cohesion and succession trickier.

Sabbaticals – approved overseas stints which allow players to take up short, lucrative stints at overseas clubs and remain available for the All Blacks – have been a compromise.

Ardie Savea, talismanic All Blacks captain, has been playing in Japan on one this season.

But, overseas clubs hungry for Kiwi talent on a longer-term basis are circling.

There is another angle to the issue that cuts against the All Blacks.

Those who do stay and remain eligible are competing in a weakened Super Rugby tournament.

South African sides left in 2020, throwing their lot in with the United Rugby Championship and the European club scene.

With only Australian sides and the Fijian Drua to compete against, Kiwi provincial sides' fixture lists are a significant step down from international rugby.

It is far from ideal preparation for the Test arena.

Then add in the cross-code lure.

New Zealand Warriors, the Auckland-based NRL side, offer a convenient and potentially lucrative route into the 13-man game for young rugby talent.

After taking a hit during Covid, grassroots rugby league numbers have ticked upwards., external Rugby union's equivalent numbers have been propped up by a rise in women's participation.

For the all-conquering All Blacks, suddenly the problems are stacking up.

Win or lose against England, they and New Zealand Rugby know they are playing a longer game. One they cannot afford to lose.

Sports.title: Qatar Grand Prix 2026: Antonelli tops second practice as Gasly crashes
Sports.text:
World champion Kimi Antonelli set the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix.

Italian Antonelli was 0.127 seconds quicker than Russell on the medium tyre, as neither driver set a time on the soft compound because of two red flags that punctuated the session.

Lewis Hamilton also came to halt after his Ferrari lost power, with a virtual safety car deployed so the marshals could come to the seven-time world champion's aid.

The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri plus Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the top five at the Lusail International Circuit, with the trio setting soft-tyre times that were more than four tenths adrift of the two Mercedes.

The first red flag was to clear gravel off the track after an incident for Ferrari's Charles Leclerc early on, while the other was to recover the Alpine of Pierre Gasly following a high-speed spin.

Frenchman Gasly hit a marker board before beaching himself after taking too much kerb at Turn 14 in the middle of the qualifying simulation runs.

The interruptions led to the second hour being extended by 13 minutes to allow drivers more time on track in the representative conditions.

"It was a productive day," said Antonelli. "We tried a lot of things on the car between FP1 and FP2, but in FP2, it seemed like we did a step back with the car.

"But it was very interesting to see how the car behaved after those changes. It's not easy."

Antonelli, who secured his maiden title in Mexico City earlier this month, was also fastest in the opening session on the mediums. Mercedes did fit the 20-year-old with the soft tyre in the first hour, but he failed to set a lap time on them.

He said he feels it will be close between himself and Russell for the race victory, but added: "You can never write off Max [Verstappen] and the others."

Norris, meanwhile, said Mercedes "were in a different category" to McLaren, highlighting the Silver Arrows "were quicker in every single corner by miles".

The 2025 world champion added: "We seem in a relatively decent position, similar on pace with Red Bull, and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I'd say it's OK."

Four-time title winner Verstappen said it had been a "difficult day" following his issues with heavy steering towards the end of the session.

"The balance of the car is probably too disconnected at the moment to go fast," he added. "It's costing us quite a bit of lap time."

Hamilton also had a moment with Verstappen that was noted by the race control. The Briton was on a flying lap when he got too close to the Dutchman, who was on a long run.

Verstappen said Hamilton had moved under braking, but the stewards decided no further investigation was needed.

The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was sixth on the timesheets, with Leclerc leading Hamilton in seventh and eighth, 1.3 seconds away from Antonelli's time.

The two Racing Bulls of British rookie Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson were ninth and 10th.

Leclerc had to head back into the garage after spinning and going through the gravel when Lawson was just ahead of him at Turn Nine.

The Monegasque driver said the car did not feel right, and the Italian team spent a chunk of time repairing the damage to the floor. After the session he said he lost control after going a little bit early on the throttle.

Ferrari arrived in Qatar after another on-track incident between Leclerc and Hamilton, this time in Las Vegas. The pair made contact and Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, with Hamilton saying on Thursday the team were facing "very, very challenging times".

Leclerc thinks this weekend could potentially be another struggle for the Italian team, who can secure second in the constructors' championship if they can retain at least a 44-point lead over third-placed Red Bull.

"A very, very difficult day. Not even on high fuel were we strong," said Leclerc.

"We are working hard but for some reason, Mercedes is so much faster than I think everyone expected. So the gaps are just a little bit strange."

Drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at the Lusail circuit, meaning teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix on Sunday, which starts at 16:00 GMT.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed, 16-corner track. Laps to the grid, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

Hamilton was told by his engineer in first practice tyre degradation was "much higher than expected" after highlighting his own issues.

Qatar and next week's finale in Abu Dhabi are going ahead as planned despite the ongoing conflict between the United States/Israel and Iran.

Sports.title: Jack Wilshere and Aaron Ramsey: The Arsenal legends on similar managerial paths
Sports.text:
Aaron Ramsey and Jack Wilshere have a lot in common.

Both were midfield prodigies. Both won the FA Cup playing for Arsenal under Arsene Wenger. Both represented their countries.

The image of the pair celebrating Ramsey's extra-time winner together in the 2014 FA Cup final against Hull City to end Arsenal's nine-year trophy drought at the time will forever be ingrained in the north London club's history.

They were teenagers when they made their Premier League debuts for the Gunners on the same day just two minutes apart as substitutes in a 4-0 win at Blackburn in September 2008.

Aged just 16 and 17, each were considered hot prospects who would go on to have excellent careers - and so it proved in many ways, even if both were restricted by injuries along the way.

Now 34 and 35, their paths cross again under different circumstances but many similarities very much still remain.

They are both in League One in their first permanent managerial jobs. And, guess what? Both their sides are in fine form and vying for promotion to the Championship.

It will be the first time they have met as permanent managers when Wilshere's Luton Town host Ramsey's Oxford United at Kenilworth Road on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

Ramsey and Wilshere have both tried to play down their reunion.

"Obviously it will be nice to see Jack again, but it's not about us," Ramsey told BBC Radio Oxford.

Except it is about them a little bit, given their 101 appearances in 10 years together in the Arsenal midfield - and as two young managers who are following almost identical paths.

Immediately after retiring from playing in July 2022, Wilshere was appointed the under-18s head coach at Arsenal, the club where he had risen from the youth academy to the first team.

Meanwhile, former Wales international Ramsey gained coaching experience towards the end of his playing career, also working with the under-18s at boyhood club Cardiff City.

Wilshere joined Norwich City as a coach for the 2024-25 season and it was at the end of that campaign he would first meet Ramsey as a manager in a remarkable twist of fate after they were both placed in interim charge of the Canaries and Bluebirds respectively.

The bragging rights went to Wilshere on that day in May last year as Norwich beat Cardiff 4-2.

"I owe him one from that," Ramsey joked.

Despite their close relationship and working towards the same objectives in the same league, they have not spoken "for a while".

"We are in a similar position at the moment, but I haven't had much dialogue with him over the last few months," said Ramsey.

"We're both fighting for the same things but, for me, it's just going out there to try and win a game of football."

Wilshere shared the same sentiment.

"It doesn't change anything for how we prepare," Wilshere told BBC Three Counties Radio on Friday.

"Of course, when I see Aaron, that'll be a nice moment. We spent a lot of good times together.

"He's had a really good start and credit to him. He's got a football brain, he's got a good career in the game and he's clearly taking that into his coaching.

"I wish him well, just not tomorrow."

Since taking over at Luton in October 2025, Wilshere has already tasted silverware, lifting the EFL Trophy at Wembley in April - a feeling he said he enjoyed more as a manager than when he was a player.

The 34-year-old guided the Hatters to seventh in League One last season, narrowly missing out on a play-off spot by a point.

Wilshere slightly edges his counterpart in terms of managerial experience, with 64 games in all competitions as Luton boss, while Ramsey has taken charge of 18 matches in his first season with the U's.

Neither could have their side in much better shape heading into Saturday's showdown.

After a stuttering start to 2026-27, Luton have won five of their past six games (D1) to climb from 16th up to fifth.

As for Ramsey, he is doing a fine job with Oxford considering the club have been under a transfer embargo since he arrived - and says he is "loving every second of it".

His side are on an 11-game unbeaten run - the second-longest across the entire Football League behind only Salford City (13).

With just one defeat so far, Oxford are third and three points behind Stockport and Huddersfield with two games in hand.

They also give a lot of credit to their role model Arteta.

Watching from afar, Ramsey previously said it was inspiring to see his former team-mate guide Arsenal to the Premier League title and Champions League final.

It was also Arteta who advised Ramsey to take his coaching badges and has continued to help him along the way.

But for Wilshere, he got to learn first hand from the Spaniard on the training ground.

"I got to see Mikel and how he coached and the influence he was having," Wilshere said last month.

"I would ask him questions, why he's doing certain things, and I started to fall in love with it and how he started to prepare training sessions.

"I was influenced by Mikel, but then I had to learn how to teach. I had to learn how to get that across, how to plan a session and how to get the outcomes that you wanted."

Ramsey made no bones about his plans when he joined Oxford in June either.

"I have a really clear way of playing, an identity that I want to create," he said at the time. "But that is built on clear principles first, underpinned by elite habits and behaviours."

That identity so far has been a team that likes to play out from the back, dominate possession and attack with verve.

Only Leicester (66%) and Stockport (62%) have had a higher average share of possession than Oxford (57%) in League One so far this season.

"I think it's evident to see why we're doing it," said Ramsey, who wants his team to take risks.

"It's not always going to be perfect. We're fully aware of that but those bits in the game where we can carve teams open - that outweighs the rest."

That approach sounds very Wenger-esque, with a sprinkling of Arteta when it comes to mindset and tweaking their tactics to suit the game on offer.

"Every week is different," he said. "But what I've liked so much about us is that we've always been able to adapt and figure out what's going on and ultimately win games of football."

Ramsey also exudes calm on the touchline, another trait perhaps borrowed from his former French boss.

Sports.title: Why snooker could be the most mentally challenging sport
Sports.text:
It is perhaps one of the most visceral and deeply human interviews that any sportsperson has ever given.

When Mark Allen, snooker's world number 11, spoke live on TNT Sports, external in October, he said he was in a "bad place", that he didn't see a future in the game, and that he was "just trying to survive".

Allen had just been beaten at the Northern Ireland Open. It was his first match since the World Championship, when in May he was one black ball away from a place in the final.

He has not spoken publicly since. In a post on social media in early November, Allen said the future is "looking brighter",, external although this week he explained he was having a "very tough" time, external and was "definitely stuck in a major low right now".

While Allen has not publicly discussed the reasons for his struggles, and if it is related to the sport, he had previously said "there is more to life than just a career".

And this would be far from the first time that poor mental health has affected a snooker player.

Right from the 1970s and the sport's first television boom, some of its great characters have spoken openly, and regularly, about addiction, isolation and snooker's unique psychological challenges.

So what is it about the sport that makes it so mentally difficult? And what is being done to help?

If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this story you can visit BBC Action Line, which has details of a range of advice and support.

In his emotional interview, Allen said he had spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic and discharged himself to play in Belfast, though he planned to continue his treatment.

Other players have also previously spoken candidly about their own struggles, including multiple world champions Ronnie O'Sullivan and Mark Selby.

Selby considered retirement after a first-round defeat at the 2024 World Championship, while in 2025 O'Sullivan said many players "suffer in silence".

Snooker is, perhaps alongside golf, one of the most intensely individual sports, where players spend long hours alone in dimly lit practice rooms or travelling on the road, and where entire livelihoods can come down to tiny misjudgements.

"At least in golf you have your own ball. You don't have to worry about anyone else," 1997 world champion Ken Doherty told BBC Sport.

"In snooker, when you're sitting in your chair and your opponent is at the table, you can do nothing. Only sit and bear it.

"That is the toughest part about our sport and mentally that is quite difficult for people to comprehend."

Dr Paul Gaffney is a psychologist who has worked with Allen for the past four seasons. Snooker players, he says, can feel like they are inside a "colosseum".

"There are people looking down at you, and you can absolutely thrive, or be beaten in front of the world stage."

Gary Wilson, the world number 28, has also spoken openly about the bouts of depression he has suffered during his 22-year career.

"It's a very lonely sport," the 41-year-old told BBC Sport.

"You're practising in a club and you could be in there on your own for six, seven, eight hours a day in a dark room, with just a snooker light on.

"It can get unhealthy mentally in itself, but it's what you've got to do. You've got to dedicate yourself to it.

"I think it is a more mentally destructive sport, potentially, than a lot of other individual sports."

When asked how he felt watching Allen's interview, Wilson said: "We can all relate.

"There are a lot of lads who are a lot lower down on the tour struggling.

"Every couple of years, this coming out and nothing being done about it, isn't really good enough."

Since 2021, snooker's governing body, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA), has put mental health provisions in place for players in the form of a partnership with Sporting Chance, a charity founded by former Arsenal and England footballer Tony Adams.

In the five years since the partnership was formed, Sporting Chance has provided more than 180 sessions of counselling for a wide range of issues.

Players experiencing mental health issues are encouraged to ring a confidential 24/7 helpline, and Sporting Chance will then arrange free treatment with a qualified therapist. This can take place over six to 12 talking sessions.

But some players believe that support could go further. In an interview in January 2025, O'Sullivan and Selby said they would like to see mental health professionals operate on-site at tournaments.

"I think players would have a lot more inclination to use somebody physically there at tournaments. I don't know how feasible that is," said Wilson.

There are benefits and drawbacks to the Sporting Chance service. Players receive a bespoke counsellor, rather than one who may speak to every player, but they are required to reach out themselves for this through a helpline. Doherty, who sits on the WPBSA players' board, believes it is the best solution.

"Players don't necessarily want to go and speak to someone at a tournament," Doherty said.

"We thought about having someone on hand, but then we thought, we don't think anyone would use it.

"This is a free service. Nobody has to know. Nobody will know on the circuit. It's just you and the person you're talking to.

"I know Ronnie [O'Sullivan] and Mark [Selby] spoke about that, but they obviously didn't know that service was there for them, that it's free, and that it's available for the whole tour."

WPBSA chairman Jason Ferguson, a former professional player himself, said: "The highs are very high and the lows are very low.

"If there's anything we can work on, it's continually getting the message out to other players to say those services are there."

In 2021, Wilson said he felt "totally gone" when the depression he explained he was suffering with came to a head in a match against John Higgins.

Wilson missed a pot, and while still down on his shot, thrashed the cue ball into a neighbouring red,, external sending the frame into chaos. He was fined £250 and received a formal warning.

But Wilson - known as the Tyneside Terror - believes there could be a more liberal approach to such displays of emotion in this most gentlemanly of sports.

"You're expected to keep your emotions completely in check at all times," he said.

"Now that's just not sport. When you look at any other sport that you play… you've got to be able to vent."

In response, Ferguson said that while snooker's authorities and fans love to see such passion, fundamentally it is a sport of "great etiquette".

Allen is next due to play in the UK Championship - a tournament he won in 2022 - which starts on Saturday. He has been drawn against qualifier Yuan Sijun but has not spoken publicly about whether he will play.

For Dr Gaffney, watching Allen's interview at Belfast's Waterfront venue was "painful". It made him feel "sadness, but also admiration".

"The brilliant thing about what he's done - his courage, his integrity, his class in the last few weeks - is there will be people watching snooker who wouldn't have been watching snooker before, because Mark Allen is playing," said Dr Gaffney, "and I think that says everything about the man."

Sports.title: Nottm Forest 3-2 Chelsea: How the players rated
Sports.text:
Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice as Nottingham Forest beat Chelsea at the City Ground for the first time since 1997.

Igor Jesus' brilliant volley opened the scoring after just five minutes, before Gibbs-White struck twice in the second half as Chelsea were consigned to a fourth defeat in five matches.

Forest ran out 3-2 winners despite Emmanuel Emegha twice pulling goals back.

Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players.

Matz Sels: The Belgian goalkeeper could do little about Emegha's goals but did not need to make many saves. 6

Jair Cunha: Cunha made one brilliant last-ditch tackle in the second half as Chelsea pushed for an equaliser. 7

Nikola Milenkovic: The Serbian was solid in the middle of the back three but otherwise unremarkable. 7

Murillo: The Brazilian centre-back made a host of important tackles and no-nonsense clearances throughout. He set the tone for a physical display and had a powerful volley saved. 7

Daniel Munoz: A typically energetic presence on the right, he also set up the opening goal. 7

James McAtee: The midfielder was good in possession but his shots lacked threat. His set-piece delivery was also poor. He did, however, win a few fouls for his team to take the pressure off. 7

Xaver Schlager: The combative midfielder set the tone early by winning the ball back in Chelsea's half on multiple occasions. He screened the backline well as Chelsea pushed for an equaliser. His wonderful pass through the eye of the needle created Forest's third. 9

Neco Williams: The Welshman battled hard with Pedro Neto in a tactical contest that ended with both players emerging with credit. 7

Igor Jesus: His sensational first-time volley opened the scoring just five minutes into the match, while the rest of his play was neat and tidy. 8

Morgan Gibbs-White: The forward scored his first goal in 11 games against Chelsea from the penalty spot in the second half. He took that chance and then another when played through by Schlager. 8

Liam Delap: The former Chelsea striker proved his worth to Forest by leading the line brilliantly, carrying a threat, looking dangerous in transition and ultimately winning a penalty for his side. 8

Dan Ndoye (on 71, Jesus)

Ibrahim Sangare (on 84, Schlager)

Chris Wood (on 84, Delap)

Subs not used: John Victor, Netz, Diomande, Yates, Hudson-Odoi, Kalimuendo

Emiliano Martinez: The Argentine goalkeeper was sent the wrong way from the spot and could not have saved Jesus' volley but made a couple of other saves. 6

Josh Acheampong: The young defender played within himself at the City Ground. 5

Wesley Fofana: The Frenchman was booed by his own supporters and told he is "not welcome here". It was a tough end to a horrible week which only got worse as he gave away the penalty having first been caught under a long ball. He was substituted in the 56th minute while also on a yellow card. 3

Moises Caicedo: A shock selection to start at centre-back for first time in his 210 games in English football, the Ecuadorian looked out of sorts with possession and in his positioning. He failed to cover for Fofana before he gave away the penalty. 5

Pep Chavarria: The Spanish full-back was an anonymous presence but did not make any obvious mistakes. 5

Romeo Lavia: The Belgian recovered from a poor touch early on to set the tempo for possession domination and his passes had real purpose. 7

Jordan Henderson: The 36-year-old was one of the weaker Chelsea performers as he filled in for now-defender Caicedo. 5

Pedro Neto: The Portuguese winger showed impressive work-rate competing with Williams, while threatened with his running in behind. His second-half shot was blocked but led to Chelsea's first goal, while his cross set up his side's second. 7

Cole Palmer: The forward was creative and highly involved for Chelsea but could not deliver that moment. It owed more to his team-mates not performing than himself. 6

Morgan Rogers: Rogers squandered multiple chances, including a huge opportunity to equalise from a corner midway through the second half. 4

Danny Welbeck: The 35-year-old striker had absolutely no service but was also completely anonymous in the first half and was taken off at the interval. 4

Emmanuel Emegha (on 45, Welbeck): An outstanding second-half display, with a brilliant touch and shot to pull one after the ball deflected into his path. He headed in a second at the far post. It raises the question about why he did not start having also scored against Leeds last weekend. 8

Levi Colwill (on 56, Fofana): The England international will be frustrated to have been dropped for a midfielder but was forced on amid Fofana's struggles and did not have much chance to shine. 5

Geovany Quenda (on 85, Henderson)

Marco Palestra (on 85, Acheampong)

Subs not used: Penders, Gusto, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao
