GeneralTab.title: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip
GeneralTab.text:
The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-bearing, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal documentary.

Discussing it at a private screening, she said it reflected the "fear, anxiety, uncertainty" shared by hundreds of thousands of people each year "who receive the words no one wants to hear" about having cancer.

The documentary, Heal, being shown on BBC One on Sunday, couldn't be further away from a stiff upper lip.

This is royal television without any palaces or carriages, it's an intense 30 minutes examining how "cancer strips everything away" and then a different kind of self-awareness emerges.

It reveals more of Catherine's inner thoughts than any of her previous speeches and we hear more from her children than ever before.

"Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. You have to go through treatment and surgeries and everything.

"But there's a much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. I think when you've had to confront your own vulnerabilities, you know, when you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite and in those moments, yes, a shift does happen," she says.

Some viewers might be left in tears, others may think it's too schmaltzy - either way, they're going to be talking about it. It packs an emotional punch, even though it's more of a self-scripted, video diary than a conventional, journalistic documentary.

"This will be a documentary that most people can relate to and will admire her for doing. There is an emotional directness that's an unusual departure," says royal commentator Prof Pauline MacLaran, of Royal Holloway, University of London.

MacLaran thinks it will connect well with the public, who will admire Catherine's "bravery".

The documentary follows Catherine's Three Peaks Challenge, in which she climbed the biggest mountains in England, Wales and Scotland in a single day, and the cameras record her driving in between and her encounters with other climbers.

This climb is a big mountainous metaphor for the difficulties, resilience and help of other people during the "scary, disorientating experience" of her treatment.

At the summit of one peak she gets voice messages from her three children - George, Louis and Charlotte - who each in turn send their love in a way that shows the closeness of their family. They also all hug and kiss later, along with Prince William, with tears being brushed away.

Those moments could be the emotional peaks that people will share, in a documentary made for the social media age.

It's also probably the most we've heard directly from the royal children.

Somewhere, the late Prince Philip will be scratching his head at how much the royals have dropped their tradition of privacy. Although we don't learn from the film the type of cancer or any details of Catherine's treatment.

"No previous generation of the Royal Family would have considered producing something like this," says Valentine Low, author and royal commentator.

"They would have been less willing to talk about illness and personal matters," he says.

But this documentary is in keeping, says Low, with a generation "that's more likely to think in terms of whether there could be a positive message from the experience".

Nonetheless, says Low, such a film-making approach, sharing their own chosen thoughts with the camera without an interviewer, still allows Catherine to "control the narrative".

And there are questions that arise. She speaks of her cancer journey being a "pilgrimage" and the need to "spend time on our spiritual health" - and it makes you wonder whether there has been a deeply religious or spiritual experience as part of her recovery.

There's a melancholy tone to the documentary, describing the impact of a "really dark time", and you wonder how this will sit alongside the expectations of her future royal life, when she will be queen.

It could also raise wider questions about the treatment, waiting times and recovery support available to the great majority of NHS patients, who do not have royal titles, but whose needs are as intense.

But we see Catherine in this documentary in hospital wards sharing experiences with other cancer patients and hearing about their hopes and fears. It's deliberately raw and unadorned in how it's presented.

There are lighter moments too, joking with her brother James as they head up the mountains.

Speaking at a screening, Catherine said the documentary was about "giving back" to people facing similar health worries and also to recognise the support of health services and charities working with patients and families.

Proceeds from the documentary, like her Three Peaks Challenge fundraiser, will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, in support of the hospital where she received treatment.

The open, empathetic tone of the documentary has been warmly welcomed by those working with cancer patients.

"Watching someone speak so openly about the fear, the hope and the long road to recovery can make a real difference to those going through it," says Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK.

"Her honesty will help many people feel less alone, and it will encourage important conversations about cancer in homes across the country."

Ceinwen Giles, co-chief executive of Shine Cancer Support, said: "The film's honesty is what makes it so powerful.

"By being open about her experience, the princess gives others a way to start their own conversations about how cancer affects every part of a person's life, particularly younger adults and those with young families."

Catherine herself says that her experience has made her think about well-being in a much more holistic way, "not just about fixing what is wrong. It is about finding balance in how we live."

"My hope is that this film will encourage compassion, showing the real value in standing alongside one another in the hardest of times," she says.

Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

GeneralTab.title: Pharmacies get new powers to swap prescriptions during shortages
GeneralTab.text:
Pharmacies are being given more freedom over the prescription medicines they can give to patients when items are out of stock.

Staff will be able to offer the same drug in a different strength or form – two 5mg tablets in the place of a 10mg pill, or a cream instead of an ointment, for example.

The change should help patients avoid repeat trips to their GP for an alternative prescription when the issue can be resolved safely and easily at the chemist.

And for the first time, children in England who miss their flu vaccination at school will be able to receive it at a pharmacy instead.

GeneralTab.title: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
GeneralTab.text:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

GeneralTab.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
GeneralTab.text:
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

articles.title: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip
articles.text:
The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-bearing, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal documentary.

Discussing it at a private screening, she said it reflected the "fear, anxiety, uncertainty" shared by hundreds of thousands of people each year "who receive the words no one wants to hear" about having cancer.

The documentary, Heal, being shown on BBC One on Sunday, couldn't be further away from a stiff upper lip.

This is royal television without any palaces or carriages, it's an intense 30 minutes examining how "cancer strips everything away" and then a different kind of self-awareness emerges.

It reveals more of Catherine's inner thoughts than any of her previous speeches and we hear more from her children than ever before.

"Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. You have to go through treatment and surgeries and everything.

"But there's a much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. I think when you've had to confront your own vulnerabilities, you know, when you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite and in those moments, yes, a shift does happen," she says.

Some viewers might be left in tears, others may think it's too schmaltzy - either way, they're going to be talking about it. It packs an emotional punch, even though it's more of a self-scripted, video diary than a conventional, journalistic documentary.

"This will be a documentary that most people can relate to and will admire her for doing. There is an emotional directness that's an unusual departure," says royal commentator Prof Pauline MacLaran, of Royal Holloway, University of London.

MacLaran thinks it will connect well with the public, who will admire Catherine's "bravery".

The documentary follows Catherine's Three Peaks Challenge, in which she climbed the biggest mountains in England, Wales and Scotland in a single day, and the cameras record her driving in between and her encounters with other climbers.

This climb is a big mountainous metaphor for the difficulties, resilience and help of other people during the "scary, disorientating experience" of her treatment.

At the summit of one peak she gets voice messages from her three children - George, Louis and Charlotte - who each in turn send their love in a way that shows the closeness of their family. They also all hug and kiss later, along with Prince William, with tears being brushed away.

Those moments could be the emotional peaks that people will share, in a documentary made for the social media age.

It's also probably the most we've heard directly from the royal children.

Somewhere, the late Prince Philip will be scratching his head at how much the royals have dropped their tradition of privacy. Although we don't learn from the film the type of cancer or any details of Catherine's treatment.

"No previous generation of the Royal Family would have considered producing something like this," says Valentine Low, author and royal commentator.

"They would have been less willing to talk about illness and personal matters," he says.

But this documentary is in keeping, says Low, with a generation "that's more likely to think in terms of whether there could be a positive message from the experience".

Nonetheless, says Low, such a film-making approach, sharing their own chosen thoughts with the camera without an interviewer, still allows Catherine to "control the narrative".

And there are questions that arise. She speaks of her cancer journey being a "pilgrimage" and the need to "spend time on our spiritual health" - and it makes you wonder whether there has been a deeply religious or spiritual experience as part of her recovery.

There's a melancholy tone to the documentary, describing the impact of a "really dark time", and you wonder how this will sit alongside the expectations of her future royal life, when she will be queen.

It could also raise wider questions about the treatment, waiting times and recovery support available to the great majority of NHS patients, who do not have royal titles, but whose needs are as intense.

But we see Catherine in this documentary in hospital wards sharing experiences with other cancer patients and hearing about their hopes and fears. It's deliberately raw and unadorned in how it's presented.

There are lighter moments too, joking with her brother James as they head up the mountains.

Speaking at a screening, Catherine said the documentary was about "giving back" to people facing similar health worries and also to recognise the support of health services and charities working with patients and families.

Proceeds from the documentary, like her Three Peaks Challenge fundraiser, will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, in support of the hospital where she received treatment.

The open, empathetic tone of the documentary has been warmly welcomed by those working with cancer patients.

"Watching someone speak so openly about the fear, the hope and the long road to recovery can make a real difference to those going through it," says Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK.

"Her honesty will help many people feel less alone, and it will encourage important conversations about cancer in homes across the country."

Ceinwen Giles, co-chief executive of Shine Cancer Support, said: "The film's honesty is what makes it so powerful.

"By being open about her experience, the princess gives others a way to start their own conversations about how cancer affects every part of a person's life, particularly younger adults and those with young families."

Catherine herself says that her experience has made her think about well-being in a much more holistic way, "not just about fixing what is wrong. It is about finding balance in how we live."

"My hope is that this film will encourage compassion, showing the real value in standing alongside one another in the hardest of times," she says.

Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

articles.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.text:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.

"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".

He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.

"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.

The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".

Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.

A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.

A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.

Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.

She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.

Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.

Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.

Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.

One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".

Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".

He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.

"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.

Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.

"So, I believe that young must mobilise."

As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

articles.title: Sunderland teen Beau-Jack Mensforth blackmailed girls to self-harm
articles.text:
This aticle contains distressing details

A "cowardly monster" who blackmailed girls across the world into self-harming for the entertainment of others has been detained for 14 and a half years.

Beau-Jack Mensforth was 17 when he began forcing vulnerable girls to send sexual images, hurt animals and carve his assumed name into their bodies, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

One of the girls' mothers said he used the internet to breach the safety of his victims' homes and minds, causing lifelong devastation.

Mensforth, 20 and from Sunderland, admitted 17 offences. They included crimes against nine victims, the youngest of whom was aged 12, and having indecent images of children as young as five.

Mensforth was in online groups who made content for their "com", short for community, by victimising "vulnerable young girls", prosecutor Charlotte Hole said.

They often targeted girls in self-harm support groups and used apps including Telegram and Discord to befriend them.

Abusers convinced the girls they were in romantic relationships and coaxed them into sending indecent images of themselves, then threatened to publish the pictures unless they committed more "extreme" acts, the court heard.

If you are affected by any issues raised, help can be found through BBC Action Line

The girls would be forced to carve the names of their abusers into their flesh and write messages and logos in blood promoting the "com" groups.

They were also ordered to "sacrifice" animals under the threat their personal information would be released online or false reports would be made to trigger armed police raids of their homes.

Under the username Yuri, Mensforth targeted girls in the UK, USA and Australia, making them write "I worship Yuri" in blood among a litany of other abuses.

When one of his victims asked him why he was doing it, Mensforth replied "for content", the court heard, with the abuser seeking to rise to the top of the group's hierarchy.

A victim from the USA said she was 16 when she was "lured" into Mensforth's "online child predator group".

Having been forced to harm herself, the pictures of her "mutilated" body then got thousands of views online, she said.

She said she begged her abusers to take the images down but they refused, adding: "The more I cried about it the more amusement it seemed to bring them."

Her mother said she had no idea there were "cowardly monsters" like Mensforth "hiding behind a screen tormenting our baby girl".

A UK-based victim, who was 13 when Mensforth began abusing her, reported him to police.

"Instead of looking back at my early teen years and being filled with joy, I'm reminded of the fear and violation I felt," she said.

Her body was "covered" with scars inflicted at Mensforth's behest, she said, describing him as a "psychopath" who "feeds off the pain" of others.

Other victims said they had ongoing mental health issues and their trauma was worse because the images were still online.

Mensforth admitted blackmail, sexual communications with children, making and distributing indecent images of children and participating in an organised crime group between 2023 and 2024.

Judge Edward Bindloss said Mensforth was a "calculating predator" who groomed, manipulated and blackmailed girls for those who shared his "taste for sexual violence and enjoyed watching females self-harm".

Mensforth "rose to play a leading role" in the harm group and "thrived" on his status, the judge said.

Bindloss said Mensforth, who told probation workers he hoped to push a girl into killing herself, would have to serve six years on extended licence.

articles.title: Charity set up in Captain Sir Tom Moore's name bids to be struck off
articles.text:
A charity set up by the family of renowned pandemic fundraiser Capt Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.

The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Sir Tom's name at the request of his family last year.

An application to have it struck off appeared on the Companies House register on Friday.

The World War Two veteran became a household name during the first Covid-19 lockdown, raising £39.4m for NHS charities by walking laps of the garden at his home in Marston Moretaine, Bedfordshire.

However, the charity founded in his name became mired in controversy after the charities watchdog found misconduct and mismanagement on the part of his daughter and her husband in their running of it.

The Charity Commission's report uncovered a "repeated pattern of behaviour" through which Hannah Ingram-Moore and her husband, Colin, made private gains and which the regulator said would have left people feeling "misled".

A £1.4m book deal and an £18,000 awards ceremony appearance fee were among the financial benefits the Ingram-Moores were found to have enjoyed through the Captain Tom Foundation.

They have already been banned from being charity trustees and earlier resigned from the foundation.

The millions raised by the late Sir Tom and donated to NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission's inquiry.

The father-of-two died aged 100 in February 2021 with coronavirus.

articles.title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
articles.text:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: Satellite imagery shows how fast Lagos and Alexandria are sinking
articles.text:
Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.

Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.

The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".

This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.

Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.

In the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.

But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.

Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days.

"[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".

The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.

The ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.

If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted, external, under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.

Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.

Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively.

Methods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops.

"Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level.

The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring.

The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested.

Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances,, external could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations".

articles.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
articles.text:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.

"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."

The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

articles.title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
articles.text:
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.

Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.

In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.

Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.

Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.

"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.

The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.

However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.

Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.

Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.

Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

articles.title: Dec Donnelly says I'm a Celebrity tension 'became much bigger deal than it should have'
articles.text:
I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here host Declan Donnelly has said tensions between Mariella Frostrup and AJ Odudu over cooking duties on the show "became a much bigger deal than it should have".

Co-host Ant McPartlin said "cooking makes things very tense in camp", adding: "If they could zoom out a little bit in there, they'll realise it's not that deep. But they just can't, once they're in there".

Donnelly and McPartlin discussed on their podcast how relations became fractious, when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode - the next day Odudu was distressed after Frostrup accused her of being "aggressive".

On Wednesday 887 people complained to Ofcom about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.

Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".

On their podcast, Hanging Out with Ant and Dec, Donnelly said tensions in camp started "surprisingly early".

"From day one cooking was tense and then it obviously came to a head with AJ and Mariella, and it spilled over to breakfast the next morning," he said.

McPartlin added: "You have 12 hungry mouths to feed and you and your sous chef, the other chef, are cooking and everyone is stood around looking at them. The pressure is quite a lot."

Donnelly continued: "When you are there, and so much of your life revolves around that mealtime, it's the only meal of the day you really get that isn't rice and beans.

"There is a lot of pressure and obviously Mariella was feeling that pressure.

"AJ wanted to come in and help and it all came to a head, and maybe because there was so much pressure and because it was so important, Mariella maybe didn't handle it very well around the campfire when she was cooking, and it spilled over into the next day - and it became a much bigger deal than it should have done."

He said the "most important thing" was that "the two ladies were able to sit down and drew a line under it, they were adult enough to sit there, talk it through, and move on together. If more people did that the world would be a much better place".

McPartlin agreed, saying: "If some of our leaders did that, the world would be a better place."

articles.title: GTA 6 crashes into top end of music chart after its record launch
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 has been swerving into online feeds and cultural conversations since its record-breaking launch last week.

But one area where the game is really making a dent is the world of music.

Flower In A Hurricane, the single from the game's official soundtrack album by Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, has climbed to number three on the UK's Official Singles Chart.

Go Easy, a new track from Dua Lipa specially recorded for the game, is the highest new entry at 21.

Seven other songs recorded for GTA 6 by artists including Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen also placed in the top 100.

Video game music has topped the UK chart before, when Robbie Williams' It's Only Us, recorded for the FIFA 2000 soundtrack, got to number one.

Run Away With Me, a 2015 song by Carly Rae Jepsen used during a "needle drop" moment in the game's first chapter, has also seen a huge spike in listeners.

It originally peaked at number 58 in the UK 11 years ago, but has re-entered the charts at number 28.

Speaking to BBC music correspondent Mark Savage, Jepsen remembered feeling the track had "something special to it" when she recorded it.

While it's a favourite among some of the singer's most loyal fans, it has never reached the level of recognition as her hits Call Me Maybe and I Really Like You.

"It never got eyes like it's getting right now," she said.

"It's just so lovely to see that happening, it makes me believe in that special feeling that we had."

There are three elements of GTA 6's soundtrack, including an official, double-sided album containing tracks recorded for the game, and an original score composed by electronic duo Justice, due to be fully released in December.

The game also features hundreds of licensed tracks on its in-game radio stations.

Flower In A Hurricane was released as a single in October, giving it time to appear on playlists in the lead-up to the game's debut.

But Mat Ombler, head of partnerships at video game music label Laced Records, says GTA 6's impact on the charts is still impressive.

He says video game soundtracks entering the album charts "isn't unheard of" but "it's incredibly rare to see multiple tracks hitting the singles charts".

Ombler likens the spike in streams of Jepsen's track to the boost Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill got from its inclusion in Netflix hit Stranger Things.

"Both tracks are part of a huge cultural moment, but I'd argue that GTA's usage of Run Away With Me is more impactful... where the music responds according to what you're doing during a key story mission," he says.

Ombler thinks the chart impact of GTA 6 highlights "the growing importance and cultural impact of video game soundtracks as a whole".

"Over 40 million people will spend the coming weeks and months listening to more than 800 tracks featured in the in-game radio stations, possibly hundreds of times," he says.

"They'll discover new music in genres they might never have engaged with otherwise, and this music will stick with them for the rest of their lives."

Only One by New York band Fcukers appears on the official GTA 6 soundtrack and has already had more than one million streams on Spotify.

The group's singer Shanny Wise tells Newsbeat: "It was actually one of the songs we recorded when we were making our album, but it didn't end up making the album."

"We felt like the vibe of it maybe was too much of an outlier," adds bassist Jackson Walker Lewis.

"But when the GTA thing came around... I felt like it perfectly fit."

Lewis says the band didn't know they'd made the official soundtrack album until the tracklist leaked in the days leading up to the game's release.

"The one thing I'll say is, Rockstar operates very fluidly behind the scenes," says Lewis.

"They can change their mind last-minute. I think that's what makes them so good at what they do is because they have flexibility."

Steven Ellison, better known as Flying Lotus, points out the GTA series was already an established cultural phenomenon.

Millions of players heard the US producer, DJ, film-maker and rapper hosting FlyLo, one of GTA 5's in-game radio stations.

He also curated its tracklist - a job he confesses was made easier by the series' profile.

"People just wanted to have any involvement at all," he says.

"It was like: 'Who do we want? Who don't we want?' It was incredible."

He says the role gave him an opportunity to "shine a light on musicians from LA", his hometown, and the inspiration for the game's fictional location Los Santos.

It also influenced his own musical taste, he says.

"I remember when I played GTA: Vice City and it was the first time I actually listened to Africa by Toto.

"I was like: 'Man this song is awesome'. I didn't really know it before."

That curated experience, according to Ellison, is a big part of the appeal, and why the game can generate surprise hits out of neglected songs.

"It's so hard to get an experience like that nowadays with the way we listen to music and find music," he says.

"So this is kind of like that experience from back in the day where you're actually being put on to something by hanging out with people and then someone plays a track.

"It's that genuine connection that I think is possible with this."

Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Jordan Kenny and Naomi Clarke.

articles.title: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
articles.text:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

articles.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
articles.text:
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

articles.title: My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
articles.text:
Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurantshe has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, shelooks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.

"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.

articles.title: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
articles.text:
The blame game for the demise of Poundland is in full swing.

The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already.

Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.

They point to improving sales over recent months as proof the business had a future.

MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".

Unsurprisingly perhaps, Gordon Brothers dispute a lot of how they have been characterised.

First, they insist that they lent the business £85m to try to keep it alive for the 17 months since they bought it. Without them, this collapse would have happened in June last year.

The £20m taken out of the business since then has mostly been interest on that loan.

Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with a year earlier, Poundland was not generating enough cash to sustain itself. Sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when Gordon Brothers bought the business - more than offsetting a £100m cost-cutting programme.

Like other retailers Poundland was hit by rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates.

In the end, argue Gordon Brothers, none of the potential buyers could meet their terms and prove they had the money and expertise to make a go of it.

Such is the discrepancy between the two versions that the chair of the Business Committee wants Gordon Brothers and the management back in front of them to get to the truth.

It is still possible that a bidder may emerge in the coming hours and days to save the business as a whole but most industry observers think that looks unlikely.

Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told the BBC: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome. I think realistically, though, there is a chance now that there will be a breakup."

Like previous busts such as Woolworths, BHS and Wilko, many of these stores will find new owners and they will need local, experienced staff.

But none of that will be much comfort to those workers facing grave uncertainty a month before Christmas, when they should be at their busiest and most needed.

Gordon Brothers specialise in situations of commercial distress. When they take on a distressed company, they try to make sure that the worst possible outcome is still one that makes money for them.

In this situation, the worst outcome would mean they get paid back £22.5m, earn interest on the loan they provided the company (secured against the company assets) and a few other miscellaneous fees.

Little wonder then that many people say they had little incentive to strain every sinew to secure a buyer. They argue they kept a business that would have collapsed last June going for another 17 months, which extended employment for thousands of workers.

But if, as some retail veterans have told the BBC, Gordon Brothers never really intended to turn this business around, why would the previous owners PepCo give them a no-lose gamble? Why didn't they do what Gordon Brothers are doing - profiting with no risk?

The answer is simple: Pepco have other businesses, which could have got tangled up in the administration of Poundland.

articles.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
articles.text:
More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.

That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.

On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.

However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

articles.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
articles.text:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.

The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.

This is the question that is most difficult to answer.

Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.

Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.

But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.

A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

That depends on who you ask.

When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.

The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.

However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.

A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".

"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."

Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.

Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.

Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.

The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.

This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.

If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.

That depends on what happens next.

Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.

But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.

As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.

Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.
