articles.title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
articles.text:
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.

Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.

He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."

They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.

Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".

"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."

Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".

Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."

In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".

US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".

Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".

Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."

She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".

The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.

When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor:

Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMT

Sounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT

articles.title: Strictly star Layton Williams says Mold transformed his career
articles.text:
Strictly Come Dancing star Layton Williams has credited living and working in a small Welsh town with transforming his career.

The Bad Education actor spent months in Mold, Flintshire, rehearsing for the role of Angel in the musical Rent, which he said marked a turning point in his career.

"I've got to be honest, before I lived in Mold, I had not a clue that Mold was a place that existed, but I completely fell in love with it," he said.

Williams, from Bury in Greater Manchester, feels so connected to the town that he insisted on having a show at the Theatr Clwyd on his upcoming tour, Layton Live.

"The producers were like, 'we've never had a specific request to go to Mold, but we will make it happen'. And I said 'Thank you'," Williams said in an interview with Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales.

The show marks the 20th anniversary of his stage debut and is a "whistle-stop musical tour" through his career, which includes musicals such as Everybody's Talking About Jamie and Cabaret.

Olivier Award-winning Williams began acting professionally in theatre aged 12, but it was in Mold where he had his first major theatre role as an adult and his unlikely love for the town began.

"There was a shift while I was there. I learned so much doing the part," he said.

"I remember it so clearly, I stayed in this gorgeous little cottage, I just had such a wonderful time there."

Williams built such a connection with Mold's Theatr Clwyd that he became an ambassador and believes he even has a seat named after him in the auditorium.

In 2025, the actor earned his Olivier Award for Best Supporting Actor in a Musical, performing opposite Port Talbot theatre star Lauren Drew in Titanique - a musical parody of the film Titanic.

The actor, who played the iceberg while Drew portrayed Celine Dion, said the pair went on an "incredible journey" together and are still good friends.

"I'm actually going to her wedding next year and I'm going to see if she can come and have a little sing song with me in Wales," he said.

Williams met his partner James, from Wrexham, at Glastonbury Festival in 2023.

It was the year that Elton John performed there, who also wrote the music for Billy Elliot.

Williams said there are many "lovely connections with Elton" in his life, including beginning his career playing Billy Elliot in London's West End.

articles.title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
articles.text:
The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.

The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.

Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".

But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.

The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.

The BBC said the partnership includes:

A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts

Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app

More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate

There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.

Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".

Met Office chief executive Penny Endersby said: "Today is a landmark moment as the Met Office and the BBC join forces to give even more people across the UK access to Met Office's accurate and trusted weather information."

She added: "Our new partnership with the BBC combines the Met Office's world-leading science with the BBC's incredible reach, giving a powerful opportunity to bring the story of our changing weather and climate to millions more people."

A previous partnership between the BBC and the Met Office ended in 2018.

Since 2018, the BBC's data for its weather forecasts has been provided by the Dutch MeteoGroup, which was later acquired by US weather services company DTN.

Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.

Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots.

Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast.

The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits.

The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.

A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms.

"As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately.

"As such we are providing more digital and localised forecasts, as well as ensuring we still have appropriate national weather bulletins across the TV and radio."

BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Breakfast and the weekday editions of BBC One's News at Six will retain their usual national weather forecasts.

articles.title: Welsh rugby legend Alyn Wyn Jones encourages men to talk about hair loss after transplant
articles.text:
Rugby legend Alun Wyn Jones has urged men to open up about hair loss, saying he was "very comfortable" talking about the fact he has had a hair transplant.

Speaking one year since his operation, the former Wales and British and Irish Lions captain said men typically do not talk about the issue, but said "a lot of people" had spoken to him about it.

"I think it's important that people know there's a lot of people out there they can talk to," he said.

Jones played 158 times for Wales and 12 for the Lions, making him the most capped rugby player in history before he retired in 2023.

Jones, 41, from Swansea, said he "wasn't conscious" about his hair loss until his playing days were coming to an end.

He spent most of his career playing for the Ospreys, before a stint for Toulon in France near the end of his career.

He said his playing career had prevented him from getting a transplant sooner because of the time off required after the procedure and then to "recover properly".

But after his retirement he said he began to learn more about it and had the operation.

He said he hoped his openness about hair loss would encourage other men to talk about the issue.

"Men in general don't talk, but I've had a lot of people talk to me about it," he said.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
articles.text:
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.

Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.

She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.

He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).

Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.

Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.

Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".

The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."

Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".

French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

articles.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
articles.text:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.

They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt, 62, argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.

The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.

"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".

The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.

It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.

Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.

Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.

Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.

Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.

They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.

It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.

articles.title: Government's antisemitism adviser launches investigation into BBC
articles.text:
The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.

Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".

He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."

The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC".

The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".

The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport told the BBC: "This government will not tolerate antisemitism. It has no place in our society.

"The BBC has a crucial role in ensuring all communities are heard and feel valued as part of our public life. That is the standard that we expect the BBC to be held to. We will consider Lord Mann's independent report carefully when we receive it."

Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019, external, said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".

"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".

"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.

"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."

The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.

He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".

His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".

Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".

He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".

He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS, which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.

The Guardian recently reported, external that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.

"We have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.

"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.

"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said in a statement that it welcomed the review into "deeply concerning" experiences of Jewish staff at the BBC.

"The BBC is an important national institution and should be setting the gold standard for an inclusive workplace and impartial broadcasting," it said.

"We stand ready to support both Lord Mann and the BBC in addressing these concerns, rebuilding confidence within the Jewish community and ensuring that the BBC sets an example for other broadcasters to follow."

Last month, Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon said the BBC had given her a £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns.

The BBC said it did not uphold allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.

In January, the BBC apologised for its use of language during coverage of Holocaust Memorial Day, saying programmes should have referred to "six million Jewish people" having been murdered by the Nazi regime, rather than "six million people" or "six million mostly Jewish people".

articles.title: Tighten your corsets! Pass the smelling salts! It’s the greatest period dramas ever made
articles.text:
Lace up those corsets and wriggle into those breeches … it’s time for a huge new TV retelling of Pride and Prejudice. Jane Austen’s classic romance will come to life once more with writer Dolly Alderton’s glitzy Netflix version, starring Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet and Jack Lowden as the self-proclaimed “first ginger Mr Darcy”.

As a new generation of fans are set to fall in love with Lizzy, Darcy and the whole Bennet clan, it’s only right to celebrate all the incredible shows that have transported us back in time. Colin Firth’s wet white shirt might fly the flag for great period drama, but there are whole other old worlds spanning all centuries out there ready to stream. Our writers share some of the very best …

Brideshead Revisited

A floppy-fringed fop in cricket whites and stripey blazer, carrying a teddy bear named Aloysius? Count me in. Granada’s 1981 adaptation of Evelyn Waugh’s novel pretty much invented an entire TV genre. Like Saltburn 40 years later (but without the grave-humping), it saw an Oxford student form a homoerotic friendship with an eccentric toff and get sucked into the drama of his dysfunctional aristocratic family.

There had been great period pieces before – most notably I, Claudius – but they were stagey affairs, filmed on wobbly sets. Brideshead was a giga-budget game-changer, bringing in the cinematic scope and lavish locations we take for granted today. Poster boys Jeremy Irons and Anthony Andrews were supported by a West End’s worth of luvvies, including “Larry” Olivier and “Johnny” Gielgud. Over 11 stately episodes, it set the gilded template for ​ye olde dramas ever since. Michael Hogan

Pride and Prejudice

Pride and Prejudice was sometimes painful to watch, as Austen’s brute romantic realities – five pillars of next-generation Bennet, consigned to shrivel in genteel destitution unless they can get someone to fancy them, and fast – met the callous 90s, where the sisters have to laugh at their desperation or else they’re a killjoy. Andrew Davies’s script was fabulous but not kind. The great houses of the English aristocracy brought an elegantly tense, here’s-what-you-could-win atmosphere; like Location, Location, Location meets Squid Game.

Consequently, there was much more riding on Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle than a plain will-they-won’t-they: their unbearably slow though entirely predictable passion (even if you’d never met the book!) had to rescue the family, the society, the viewer, the very blades of grass all around, from the stress of a world in which the stakes were both impossibly high and pitiably trivial. And they really, really delivered: Ehle’s expression, as she’s almost winded by genuine feeling, is exquisitely evocative. Firth, of course, was never able to erase the cultural mark he made by jumping into a lake with his shirt on. The pair had a brief fling during and after filming, almost (one imagines) as a courtesy to the cultural fervour they created. It didn’t last, but it would have been rude not to. Zoe Williams

Technically, it can’t be done. You cannot take over a 1,000 pages of the most luminous, intricately woven prose ever written, put them on screen and lose nothing in translation – or at least nothing you don’t gain back tenfold elsewhere.

But that is what writer Peter Straughan and director Peter Kosminsky, plus a handful of actors at the top of their game, did when they adapted the first two volumes of Hilary Mantel’s trilogy about the rise and fall of Thomas Cromwell, and how he oversaw Henry VIII’s split from Rome, marriage to Anne Boleyn and eventually resolved on a scaffold at dawn the king’s Great Matter once and for all. There’s simply nothing like it – for beauty, for delicacy, for horror, for heartbreak. Every line, every frame, every fleeting expression on an actor’s face does double, triple duty as an engine of story and creator of an experience that allows you to watch the past unspool as if for the first time and stands as a testament to human creativity and the power and refuge of art. Lucy Mangan

Bleak House is the celestial moment when BBC period drama, the baronet of its adaptation for the screen Andrew Davies, the enormous cast of characters, and Charles Dickens himself were all at their very best. The outcome is 15 exquisitely taut, tense, addictive, fog-ridden half-hour episodes (except the first one which was an entire glorious hour), restoring Dickens to the serial format that made him so famous, broadcast twice weekly with cliffhanger endings so finely judged even the Victorians would have approved. Anna Maxwell Martin, in her first lead role, delivers an astonishing performance as Esther Summerson. Gillian Anderson’s haunting (and haunted) Lady Dedlock is unforgettably sombre and devastatingly sad. Charles Dance’s Tulkinghorn is the most terrifyingly serpent-like family lawyer known to the profession, all hooded eyes and hissed threats. And there will never be a more comically spot-on Mr Guppy in televisual history than Burn Gorman. Millions tuned in every week to see how Jarndyce and Jarndyce would pan out (badly, of course). I still rewatch it every single year, hanging on every perfectly-paced word. The benchmark of grip-the-nation British period drama, then and now. Chitra Ramaswamy

Period dramas are so firmly associated with bonnets and windswept moors that suggesting anything that doesn’t fit that description feels faintly sacrilegious. But despite depicting an era maybe even your mum can just about remember, and being [drops monocle into snifter in horror] American to boot, Mad Men is a proper period drama. And not just because the costumes are on point – though they are, with every last Sterling Cooper employee’s pocket square positioned just so.

No, what makes Matt Weiner’s ad industry saga so great is its ability to make its chosen age – buttoned-down late 50s giving way to the charged, chaotic 60s – both alien and achingly close to home. After all, nostalgia, as Don Draper reminded us in the show’s most memorable sales pitch, translates as “the pain from an old wound”. It’s a show that both seduces and repels you with its vision of the not-so-distant past – capitalism starting to curdle, sexism and racism both casual and deeply ingrained. But like an appealing if inadvisable Old Fashioned, you can’t help yourself from drinking it down. Gwilym Mumford

The Crimson Petal and the White

In truth, I have always struggled with period dramas, since it’s as if all the fun stuff – the characters, the plot, the identifiable human behaviour – is obscured behind a thick screen of frills and waffle. But Lucinda Coxon’s 2011 adaptation of Michel Faber’s novel cuts straight through all that. It’s a queasy, bilious four-parter that heaves with fury from the outset. Romola Garai plays Sugar, a sex worker fuelled by hatred for all the men who casually abused her and her friends. Chris O’Dowd plays William Rackham, an ineffectual rich kid who wants to be a writer but has no talent for it. He falls for her, despite having a mentally ill wife at home, and invites her to become the governess to his daughter. Sugar gets to see all the opportunities afforded to the upper classes and maximises upon them, while William stumbles into a trap of his own making. The Crimson Petal and the White represents period dramas at their nastiest. If only more would follow suit. Stuart Heritage

Any Brontë fan who has walked around the tiny, rickety rooms of the sisters’ Haworth home will have spent hours imagining the young women huddled together, scratching away with pens to tell their stories. Leave it to Sally Wainwright to put her ideas of them on screen in this exquisite feature drama about Charlotte, Emily and Anne – and their brother Branwell, whose alcoholism deeply affected their lives and works. It shows not just their fight to get published, using pseudonyms, but their increasingly desperate need to earn money as unmarried women. Filmed in a replica of the Brontë parsonage and on the surrounding Penistone Hill Country Park, it’s like living daily life and walking the moors with the sisters – played almost precisely how I picture them by Finn Atkins, Chloe Pirrie and Charlie Murphy. Forget Margot Robbie in red latex! This is the real Brontë experience. Hollie Richardson

Tipping the Velvet

It has been almost 25 years since it aired on BBC Two, and in many ways, Andrew Davies’ adaptation of Sarah Waters’ debut novel does look and feel of its time. It told the story of fictional Victorian music hall star and male impersonator Nan Astley, whose lesbian awakening dragged her through the highs and lows of London’s bohemian society. It was raucous, camp and surprisingly sexually frank. It may have cast pretty, overtly feminine women in roles that would, today, demand a more butch presence, but in the early 00s, it was a rare case of a period drama, or any drama for that matter, that did not skirt around its queerness. As such, it deserves its place in TV history. Also fun to spot Benedict Cumberbatch and Sally Hawkins and Monica Dolan in early roles, and to wonder how “Monsieur Dildo” ever made it on to the screen in 2002. Rebecca Nicholson

Our Friends in the North

We tend to think of period drama as telling stories from a century or more before and coming from a dead writer’s book. Peter Flannery’s nine-parter was adapted from his own stage play with a narrative starting 32 years before the transmission date and ending just one year before. Yet all other qualifications of the genre are met: the popularisation of distant history (in this case, civic corruption in the north east), spectacular work by the costume and wig departments, characters of Dickensian richness that four young actors – Gina McKee, Daniel Craig, Mark Strong, Christopher Eccleston – made glorious calling cards: the show’s alumnae include a James Bond (Craig) and a Doctor Who (Eccleston) and the four share a heavy shelf of Bafta, Emmy, Olivier and Tony wins and nominations. Mark Lawson

The Red Riding trilogy

“To the North. Where we do what we want!” In period terms, this three-part adaptation of David Peace’s titular trilogy is riveted tightly to Britain in the 1970s. The original novels were loosely inspired (if that’s the right word for the ambient horror they conjure) by the hunt for the Yorkshire Ripper. These dramas pick up that deadly trail and run with it, into purgatory and beyond. The police station resembles the inside of a smoker’s lung. Straight-dealers end up in metaphorical and sometimes literal ditches. And around every corner, there’s a moral dead end waiting. The cast – which includes Andrew Garfield, Rebecca Hall, Sean Harris, Daniel Mays, Maxine Peake and Paddy Considine – is extraordinary and taken as a whole, Red Riding represents a relentlessly claustrophobic suite of desolation and corruption. Bodices and frilly frock coats are conspicuous by their absence. Phil Harrison

Parade’s End, a sumptuous adaptation of Ford Madox Ford’s quartet of novels of the same name, aired on BBC Two when I was 16, just at the point when my TV tastes were becoming refined enough for meaty, sexy fare. I was blown away by Tom Stoppard’s expert take on Ford’s twisty story, which follows righteous aristocrat Christopher Tietjens as he serves in the first world war. And what a cracking cast: Benedict Cumberbatch plays Tietjens, Adelaide Clemens is excellent as Valentine Wannop, the young suffragette for whom he develops feelings, while Anne-Marie Duff and Stephen Graham appear in supporting roles. It’s Rebecca Hall, though, as Sylvia, Tietjens’s mesmerising and manipulative – but ultimately miserable – wife, who steals the show. Being closeted at the time, I put my teenage obsession with the show down to a crush on Cumberbatch, but I knew deep down it was actually Hall I fancied, with her long tailored coats and ability to express five emotions with the smallest raise of an eyebrow. I defy anyone watching Parade’s End not to fall in love with her. Lucy Knight

“It’s 1973, almost dinner time. I’m havin’ ‘oops!” growls DCI Gene Hunt (Philip Glenister) as he pins bewildered noughties metrosexual DI Sam Tyler (John Simm) against a filing cabinet in the first episode of the BBC’s still mindblowing police procedural Life on Mars. I generally find costume drama a bit too much like homework. For Life on Mars, I make an exception. That’s mainly because it’s a show about suspension of disbelief. Has Simm’s detective really time-travelled from 2006 or is he comatose, dreaming? Could his subconscious have cobbled together a vision of the past this credible? This is a show that encourages you to question every little detail of the seductive 1970s setting – a deconstruction of the period drama that reflects on nostalgia, the nature of reality and the strangeness of the past. Now, 20 years on, it’s technically a relic itself – but this postmodern masterpiece is far from dusty. Rachel Aroesti

Pride and Prejudice is on Netflix from Thursday 3 December

articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers review – phone-free arena show is a cosmic, communal revelation
articles.text:
The giant white dome that hangs over Phoebe Bridgers’ stage looks like Disney World’s Epcot, Walt’s “experimental prototype community of tomorrow” envisioning how we might live better. Bridgers’ tour is its own utopia: everyone’s phones are locked away, an edict that caused some controversy among younger fans who have never experienced a gig any other way. Down our aisle, none of us know the time and two teenage fans wearing skeleton outfits (Bridgers’ old stagewear staple) faux-complain that they’ve actually had to talk to each other.

It’s so unusual not to see a speckle of screens at an arena show that, from the seats looking down on the standing area, it feels as if there’s been some kind of power cut, or we’re in a protected natural dark reserve. The decision seemed made to protect the sanctity of the pain in Bridgers’ third album. Lost Weekend swims in her conflicted feelings over her sometimes-estranged father’s death, given his abuse of her mother, and the end of Bridgers’ fairytale engagement, after she realised she wanted something different.

The dome lifts to reveal a black-clad Bridgers and her nine-piece band, led by Melina Duterte of Jay Som, who play beautifully orchestrated, faithful versions of these songs. They tap into the Sufjan/National school of ornate crescendo, but nothing is being unduly dressed up here, or inflated to mirror Bridgers’ stature as a generational, Grammy-winning songwriter and conspicuous influence on pop stars from Taylor Swift to Gracie Abrams.

What’s miraculous is how Bridgers has transformed melancholy, silvery alt-rock into something that hits on the level of pop music, yielding feral screams from the crowd for Elliott Smith-worthy interiority. The production is the only pop thing about the show: later tilted high above the band’s heads, the dome’s concave insides turn into a sort of crystal ball, showing hazy visions of Bridgers, planets and black holes – maybe the alien, cosmic hugeness of a complicated and irreconcilable grief.

Bridgers’ restraint in not trying to fill the 23,000-capacity room means that when she and the band really lock in, it takes your hair clean off. Kill Me goes from a stunned wisp to furious, slamming drums, prompting the dome to rise up, beaming spaceship-style lights from its rim. She moves to the B-stage for Lost Weekend’s title track, sitting cross-legged on the floor at a small organ. When the bass floods and then breaks, the lights strobe Bridgers in white as she howls to the rafters: one minute she’s there, then she’s not, a faltering ghost. Glitter rains down for the belting climax of As Above, which feels something like being flayed.

With the exception of new-love anthem Bobby, these are not particularly cheerful songs (in case you couldn’t tell by the pearlescent tears painted on Bridgers’ face). You can imagine how she might have anguished about reliving their griefs and disappointments night after night. She’s talked about her discomfort at being reduced to a sad-girl meme; some fans thought it was OK to harass her in the airport en route to her dad’s funeral. She would have been well within her rights to put her guard up for life. Notably, she’s given no interviews about this album.

But aside from the lasers and dry ice, the most striking element of the show is how purely happy Bridgers looks, more so than on any previous tour. She looks genuinely pumped at the huge singalong to Motion Sickness: given recent events, hearing 23,000 young people roaring along to a song denouncing emotional abuse by an older man, is worth getting pumped over. She legs it across the main stage, beaming at the nosebleeds. The phone ban seems as much about preserving the sanctity of her happiness from commodification.

Part of Bridgers’ USP is that, for all her emotionally annihilating songs, she’s extremely funny. When she asks who has conservative parents, she gets a fairly muted response. “That’s much more universal in the US,” she says, then nods to the gig’s Manchester soil. “You guys have Morrissey. He’s everyone’s conservative parent.” She says she’s happy her UK tour means she can dodge Thanksgiving – “celebrating the genocide of people we stole the country from” – and says that for all her differences with her dad, she’s grateful they shared those values. “I never had to teach myself critical thinking.”

Alone on acoustic guitar, she plays Still Standing, her complex memorial to him, and the widespread sobbing is audible. It’s manifestly a devastating song, but something about the lack of phones seems to heighten the response. Taking away fans’ ability to turn away from hard feelings feels like a gift that forces a quality of attention: maybe the space theme hints at how disquietingly alien it feels to have nowhere to run, to see what comes up when you stare discomfort in the face. Bridgers has made her career doing it.

After the communal scream-fest I Know the End, she returns to the B-stage for an encore. Now dressed in white, she sings Scott Street sitting on the floor, and the house lights come on as everyone sways, arms in the air, looking giddily at one another after two hours of being locked in. The lack of video emerging from these gigs protects Bridgers’ privacy, but if you’re down to submit to the terms of her magic kingdom, you can see everything.

articles.title: DJ Tink, drop the beat! Peter Pan hits Club NVRLND for some noughties nostalgia
articles.text:
How about if Peter Pan, refusing to grow up, was a stunted man-boy lost in the what-ifs of his youth? He might be the promoter of a noughties club night, stuck in his glory days where everyone’s dressed like Girls Aloud meets the Vengaboys and the world hasn’t yet gone into meltdown.

NVRLAND is that club, and this show – created by Steven Kunis and Jack Holden – is halfway between a jukebox musical and a cheesy disco, masterminded, surely, for the Christmas party crowd to down oversweet cocktails before oversharing with someone they barely know from the finance department. It’s basically pantomime for millennials/zillennials, with lots of audience participation from the dancefloor. And after a bit of warming up, it is great, giddy fun.

Diana Vickers (of X Factor circa 2008, perfect casting) plays Wendy, in a wedding dress. She has just jilted an unknown fiance at the altar and is being consoled by mother of the house Tiger Lily (Le Fil). Wendy is soon swept into the nocturnal life of the club and all its Lost Boys (that’s us) as well as her old flame Peter (George Renshaw), their interpersonal agonies soon overshadowed by the villainous Croc and Hook chasing them for rent.

The drama is neatly tied to the lyrics of a hit-filled playlist: Bon Jovi’s It’s My Life, Gnarls Barkley’s Crazy and so on. For all it feels wayward, the show is tightly structured and performed. The dancers go at it with steamrolling energy, script and moves borrowing from the queer ballroom scene. The singers belt their hearts out – Vickers is very good, as is Ceili O’Connor as DJ Tink. And the rest of us shout-sing along with Avril Lavigne’s Sk8er Boi and Britney Spears’ Toxic.

It’ll make you think about the nuances of pop culture, so partisan – the few years’ difference between having a near-spiritual experience to a Coldplay song and rolling your eyes at all the phone torches held aloft. Your enjoyment will be directly in proportion to your own participation, but it does have something to say: we can revel in the escapism of nostalgia, but we can’t stave off growing up for ever.
